### 1. Cache Engineering for Agents (arXiv 2610.28577)
- what: Proposes "cache engineering," where an agent issues `drop` (exclude KV entries from attention) and `repos` (re-rotate retained keys' RoPE positions) without rewriting the text trajectory or re-prefilling, and ships AKV, a SGLang-based serving engine with an extended radix tree and segment-batch attention to support it.
- read: full (text supplied in the message; no URL was fetched, and the paper's own text was the source for this rating)
- key numbers: Tool-response rolling-drop (keep last 12 tool responses) vs. Standard summarization: cost −27.7% and avg score +1.3 to +2.1 points per model (Table 1, averaged over 4 benchmarks, Standard baseline 96K threshold). Serving on 80 SWE-Verified tasks, GPT-OSS-120B, A800s: output throughput 1.18× and P95 latency 1.51× vs. Standard at each method's peak concurrency (Table 2). Table 4 ablation: BCP 55% → 62% when `repos` is added to tool-drop.
- code/weights: Code at https://github.com/thu-nics/AKV (stated in the abstract). No model weights; uses public GPT-OSS-120B, MiniMax-M2.7, MiroThinker-1.7-Mini.
- practical: MEDIUM
- why: The core policy (drop old tool-response KV, keep reasoning) is simple, but it requires serving-side KV control that a hosted API does not expose, so the gain is only directly usable if he runs his own inference stack (SGLang-class). The cost numbers are computed from list prices with repos charged at cache-hit rate, and the headline results are on 100-task subsets with one judge (GLM-5.2), so treat the 1.3–2.1 point gains as directional. The transferable design point for Muninn is to prefer dropping stale tool outputs over summarizing the whole history when the harness can do so.

### 1. LiFT: Loop Flow Transformers (2610.05538)
- what: Trains a looped DiT core where each loop is supervised at a point on a straight path from the prelude's initial velocity estimate to the flow-matching target, and then scales inference loops beyond training depth on ImageNet 256 class-conditional generation.
- read: full (text supplied in the message; no URL was given for the paper itself, so the arXiv ID 2610.05538 is the only pointer)
- key numbers: L/2 R10 trained at 2 loops goes from FID 20.30 to 10.95 at 8 inference loops (50 steps). Against dense XL/2 at 250 steps (FID 14.30, 59.31 TFLOPs), LiFT L/2 R10 at 8 loops reaches 10.95 at 28.24 TFLOPs with about 60% fewer parameters (the paper's own accounting). At 25 steps and 4 loops, LiFT L/2 R10 gets FID 13.16 at 7.40 TFLOPs versus dense L/2 at 16.94 and 8.07 TFLOPs.
- code/weights: not stated. The abstract and page header say "Coming Soon" for the project links, and no repository is named in the text.
- practical: LOW
- why: The result that matters for you is the allocation finding: at fixed budget, trading integration steps for loops beat more steps, and the endpoint-only inference path means the checkpoint is a drop-in for a sampler. Adoption is blocked, though, because this is a ~1B-scale class-conditional ImageNet DiT trained on 4×H100 for 500k updates, with no code or weights. The FID comparisons are single runs with no CFG, and the paper's own B/2 results show the dense model still wins at the smallest scale. The idea of putting distinct targets on loops is worth a note for anyone designing looped small models, but it does not change a routing or retrieval decision you can make this month.

### 1. Embodied Turing Machines: Stateful Code for Robot Recursive Self-Improvement (2610.12369)
- what: Proposes Code-Only-as-Policy (COAP), a frozen, model-free code library that tracks robot and object state from RGB and proprioception, with coding agents improving the code offline; reports 70.24% on RoboDojo's 42 bimanual tasks, in simulation.
- read: full (text supplied in the message; no URL given for the paper itself) — the full text was provided, so I rated from the paper's own content.
- key numbers: 70.24% overall SR on RoboDojo vs. 31.38% for the best leaderboard entry (PhysicalRSI, agent+VLA) and 27.96% for the best VLA; COAP runs a control step at a median 0.3 ms on a CPU. Oracle-state success is 83% vs. 63% on measured state, which means the perception gap is the main limit.
- code/weights: not stated. The paper mentions no released code, library, or weights.
- practical: LOW
- why: Its key claim of 70% comes from a simulator benchmark with simulator-derived camera, mesh, and object constants, and it reports that these must be re-measured for real robots. Development used Opus 5.5 coding agents running for many hours per task, and the paper gives no cost figure for that. The one finding that changes a design decision is the framing that a frozen, explicitly-stateful rule layer with an offline-only model can handle routing-like decisions without a model at runtime. This is a robotics result, though, and I'd only borrow the state-tracking-plus-offline-code pattern, not the method itself.

### 1. Harness^2: Recursive Agent Harnessing for an Open World (arXiv 2610.14224)
- what: Proposes Harness^2, a label-free method that refines an agent's execution harness per task via a contrastive Propose–Probe–Compose step (parallel or sequential recursion), and updates a separate improvement-harness library after each task so later tasks benefit.
- read: full (text supplied in the request; no URL fetched)
- key numbers: One step at k=1 gives GLM-5 WorkBuddy-Bench Avg 75.7 vs 64.2 base under OpenCode (+11.5); LAB Partial +11.8 for GLM-5. Parallel recursion at k=5 adds 2.9–3.9 on WorkBuddy-Bench. Leave-one-out ablation: removing the library drops WorkBuddy-Bench 77.5→74.4. Harness-scaling and ReasoningBank baselines are reported in the same tables.
- code/weights: Repo github.com/google-research/harness2 and project page harness2.github.io are stated in the paper. No weights (the executors are frozen third-party models).
- practical: MEDIUM
- why: The contrastive Propose–Probe–Compose loop and the rule that every skill must be named in always-on text, with scripts shipped alongside it, are concrete design patterns you can copy into a Muninn skill-authoring or harness-edit workflow. Costs are real, though: k=5 parallel recursion means several extra executions and editor sessions per task, and the paper uses Claude Opus 4.8 as editor, so the cost trade-off against your cheap-subagent routing is not settled. The gains are also sensitive to ±3–5 point run variance, and the paper's own failure analysis shows selection and shared-model-bias errors.

### 1. Next-Concept Modeling: Fast, Parallel Coarse-to-Fine Text Generation (2610.14162)
- what: Trains a multiscale residual VQ-VAE to turn text into a coarse-to-fine hierarchy of discrete codes, then a ~100M transformer generates each level in parallel (K≪L steps), with an MBR candidate-selection option at inference.
- read: full (text supplied in the message; no URL was given for the fetch, the paper text was provided directly)
- key numbers: LM1B ~21× faster wall-clock than DUO at better Gen. PPL (93.05 vs 97.30 at 12 vs 128 NFE, Table 8); XSum ROUGE-L 28.0 at 8 NFE vs AURORA-LM 26.6 at 128 NFE (no guidance); Sudoku hard 86.1% vs FMLM+ 81.3%.
- code/weights: GitHub link stated (https://github.com/HazyResearch/ncm); weights not explicitly stated.
- practical: LOW
- why: The core idea (residual multiscale VQ, parallel per-level decoding) is a design pattern worth knowing, but adopting it means training a tokenizer plus a generator per dataset, and the headline speedups are measured against diffusion baselines rather than the AR-with-KV-cache setup the reader actually runs. Results are at ~100M scale on small benchmarks (LM1B, TinyStories, a 1024-token OWT setting), with a self-reported Gen. PPL metric that the paper itself caveats for diversity effects. Nothing here changes routing or cost decisions for Muninn, and the tokenizer-plus-generator training budget is well beyond a weeks-long replication.

### 1. TokenRouter: Efficient Serving System for Token-Level LLM Routing (2610.12242)
- what: Proposes a serving runtime (built on SGLang) for token-level LLM routing, with one subserver per model, a route-send-receive programming interface, a pending/resume handoff that preserves KV state across model switches, and a delayed-batching scheduler whose threshold is chosen from a DTMC throughput model.
- read: full (text supplied in the request; no URL fetched). Code link is in the paper's abstract.
- key numbers: 2.01–64.15× throughput over the "stronger" baseline across 15 algorithm–workload combinations (Figs 5–6). Against official R2R at concurrency 4 (Table 2), 244.56 vs 89.62 tok/s, a 2.73× gain. Against the R2R official code at concurrency 8, the ablation goes 134.9 → 372.5 tok/s, a 2.76× gain. The headline 64× figure is the stronger baseline's worst case, not a typical result.
- code/weights: GitHub link stated (https://github.com/thu-nics/TokenRouter). Model weights are the public Qwen3 models; no new weights.
- practical: MEDIUM
- why: If you run a cheap-model/expensive-model split in your own agent, the handoff-resume idea (don't re-run prefix matching when a routed token comes back) and the "measure your own batch-admission delay before you pick a batch threshold" lesson are both transferable to a SGLang/vLLM setup within weeks. The headline numbers are heavily shaped by the weak baselines (the Co-LLM official code at 3.46 tok/s, and the R-Stitch comparison with no official code), and the throughput model's own validation is on a single pair (R2R, M=2, one value of p); treat the 64× as a ceiling, not a forecast.

- what: Converts 100k anonymized social-platform user behavior histories into 75k SFT tasks (Predictive and Rubric questions scored against hidden future behavior), fine-tunes Qwen3.6-35B-A3B on them, and reports gains on user-related and general benchmarks.

- what: Learns an offline textual "Meta-Skill" from A/B/C rollout contrasts (no evolver, evolver guided by the current Meta-Skill, evolver with privileged verifier info), then freezes it and uses it at test time to decide KEEP or task-local EVOLVE edits at checkpoints inside a run, resetting the harness to the seed for every run.

- what: Proposes CoworkOS, a harness that splits a Main agent (strategy/acceptance) from a Coordinator runtime and delegated Subagents, adds shared-resource editing for documents, CAD and Blender, workspaces with persistent memory, and background Jobs, then reports benchmark results and a five-round automated post-training run.
- read: full (text supplied in the request; no URL fetched) — the paper's own text, including appendix tables and the stated repo link.
- key numbers: Tool Use average 55.22 vs DSH 55.31 and OpenHands 51.33; Productivity 57.54 vs DSH 56.13; the RSI run takes Qwen3.6-35B-A3B from 33.19 to 42.95 over 8 benchmarks (+9.76), with no variance or repeated-seed numbers.
- code/weights: repo at github.com/RUC-NLPIR/CoworkOS and project page are stated; no model weights or training data release is stated.
- practical: LOW
- why: The architecture (Main/Coordinator/Subagent split, revision-checked `Commit` with conflict on stale base revision, Inbox-based async delegation, checkpointed Jobs) is a useful design pattern for your Muninn memory and delegation layer, and I'd name the revision-conflict rule as the one thing worth copying. But the headline results are single-run, the model being evaluated is a 35B MoE with an unreleased backbone (GLM-5.3), and the baselines are run under the authors' own configs, so the harness-vs-harness margins (often under 1 point) can't be used to pick a harness. The post-training gain also mixes concurrent interventions per round, which the authors themselves concede, so it doesn't isolate what the harness contributed.
